title: Playing soft: the subtle swing
summary: Without amplification the band played quietly and used dynamics.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: How could you get sounds like low register clarinet and bass clarinet across, say in a live situation, without amplification?
I don't think they went in so much for huge auditoriums, where

you got millions of people; they didn't do that. If you did--they had some in Madison Square, but I think already they were using amplification of an awful sort. It didn't mean very much, but mostly I think they were smaller rooms, nightclubs.

Sometimes other people would play soft too, and in those days Benny got kicked out of an east side hotel he was playing for playing too loud. People wanted to talk, so the emphasis was on playing softly, and we really did play soft whether you did it on a clarinet or a saxophone didn't make very much difference. It was more difficult to play soft on a trumpet.
That was any specialty of Red's. They used to call us the subtle swing.
Sure; but it was very soft. I've always been attracted to that, we used to try to have dynamics in
soft and some of the most exciting things were very very soft, like a whisper sometimes, to come down from something loud into that.
